title: A hanging chain showed in the 1740s that the cracked dome of St Peter’s would stand
body: Michelangelo redesigned the dome of [St Peter’s Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Basilica) in 1547, and Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana finished it in 1590: two brick shells with 16 ribs, 41.5 m across inside. By the 1740s long cracks ran up from its base, splitting it into slices that behaved like separate arches. In 1742–43 three mathematicians, Thomas Le Seur, François Jacquier and Roger Boscovich, studied it and called for heavy strengthening; Pope Benedict XIV then turned to [Giovanni Poleni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Poleni) of Padua. Poleni used Robert Hooke’s idea: a hanging chain is pulled only by tension, so its shape turned upside down is a path along which weight travels in pure **compression**. He hung weights in proportion to the pieces of one slice on a chain and found that the flipped curve fitted inside the dome’s thickness, so each slice could stand. The danger was the slices’ **outward push** at the base, held by iron rings like hoops on a barrel: six were added in the 1740s, after one of the old rings was found broken. Poleni published his analysis in 1748.

slides.question: In the 1740s, how many new iron rings were put round the cracked dome of St Peter’s Basilica?
slides.explanation: Six, after the architect Luigi Vanvitelli found one of the dome’s old rings broken. Giovanni Poleni had shown the cracked dome would stand if its outward push was held.

slides.alt: Animation at dusk: St Peter's dome, cracks running up from its base, seen from above as slices. A hanging chain turns over into an arch; one slice of the dome is cut into pieces, a chain hung with matching weights flips into a line that fits inside the masonry; iron rings go round the dome.
slides.music: “Despair and Triumph” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Set the outward push at the base until the line of thrust, Poleni’s chain turned over, fits inside the slice of masonry.
slides.takeaway: Only a narrow range of pushes keeps the line inside the 3 m of masonry: then the slice can stand, as Poleni found. That outward push is what the drum and the iron rings must hold.

slides.alt: The dome of St Peter’s Basilica against a blue sky: lead-covered between pale stone ribs, crowned by its lantern, ball and cross, rising behind the statues on top of the basilica’s façade.

steps.label: See the cracked dome as slices
Hang a weight for each piece on a chain
Turn the chain’s curve upside down
It fits in the masonry: the slice stands

events.text: Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana finish it.
Pope Benedict XIV calls in Poleni.

slides.question: Why could a hanging chain tell Giovanni Poleni whether the cracked dome of St Peter’s was safe?
options: Its weight equals the dome’s weight
It measures how wide the cracks are
It stops the dome from spreading
slides.explanation: A chain carries only tension. Turned upside down, its curve is a path along which the slice’s weight travels in pure compression; if that path stays inside the masonry, the slice can stand.

source.label: Funari et al. (2021): Structural stability of St Peter’s dome
